extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and readers interested in history of technology, media studies, and cultural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical criteria for evaluating futurist rhetoric and the social/ideological effects of communications technologies (with a focused case study of the telegraph). Emphasizes how technological promises, organizational forms, and discourse shape politics and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary potential beyond prosaic facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The revolutionary potential attributed to communications improvements does not derive from prosaic facts (more information sent faster), but from their supposed capacity to transform the commonplace into the extraordinary: create new communities, new politics, new standards of efficiency, and usher in a 'new man'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims about communications technologies by asking whether assertions rest merely on technical improvements or on grand transformative promises (e.g., complete democratic renewal, eradication of ignorance). Beware rhetoric that equates greater speed/fidelity with inevitable moral/social progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Futurean mirage / teleological future
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'futurean mirage' is the conception of the future as an active agent reaching back into the present and past, revising time and removing obstacles to a predetermined destiny; it posits the future as already out there and converging with history's final stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat portrayals of the future as preordained or as an autonomous agent with skepticism. Such teleological framing is an ideological device that forecloses alternative futures and masks political choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between information and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Information (bits/data) is often conflated with knowledge, but knowledge is paradigmatic and structured by conceptual systems; information devoid of conceptual frameworks cannot by itself constitute knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims about information technologies, explicitly examine the paradigms, categories, and conceptual assumptions embedded in systems. Do not accept assertions that access to more data automatically equals full knowledge or understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two senses of 'monopoly of knowledge'
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopoly of knowledge can mean (1) control of factual information/data flow, or (2) control of the entire system of thought (paradigm) that defines what counts as fact and reasonable; the latter is more stringent and politically consequential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between ownership/control of data and control over interpretive frameworks. Evaluate whether technologies centralize only data or also legitimate and enforce a technocratic worldview that defines acceptable knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technocratic/elitist capture and monopoly tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: New communication technologies are often aligned with technocratic elites who monopolize knowledge, managerial power, and decision-making—producing centralization, uniformity, and erosion of political/community life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a technology's institutional deployment enhances decentralization and public empowerment or instead concentrates control in specialist/technical elites (scientists, technocrats, corporations, military-industrial interests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation as ritual or legitimizing device
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of public engagement around futures (World Games, Delphi techniques, surveys, electronic voting schemes) often function as ritualistic participation that legitimates pre-decided plans rather than enabling genuine democratic influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate participatory processes for authenticity: are outcomes open and contestable, or are participatory forms used to rubber-stamp expert-determined policies? Look for asymmetries in who sets agendas and who interprets results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Futurist literature as a cultural strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The literature of the future acts as a cultural strategy to mobilize people toward predefined ends by prescribed means, selectively deleting inconvenient aspects of the past and present and legislating preferred plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize futurist texts for selective omission, rhetorical devices that erase conflicting evidence, and appeals that mobilize consent for particular programs. Ask who benefits from the proposed future and what is being silenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfalsifiability and revisability of futurist claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Futurists can always rewrite the future because there is no systematic verification of prophecy and no record against which to compare predictions; the future can be postponed or redefined when predictions fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat broad predictive claims as lacking empirical accountability. Favor analyses that specify mechanisms, testable assumptions, and criteria for evaluation rather than open-ended prophecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three enunciations of the future (exhortation, prophecy, ritual)
rubrics_metrics.description: The future enunciates the present in (1) exhortation (encouraging faith in an imminent future), (2) prophecy (descriptive forecasts written as inevitabilities), and (3) ritual of participation (inviting the public to partake in constructing the future).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which enunciative mode is being used in a text or campaign; each mode carries different rhetorical functions and vulnerabilities to manipulation or depoliticization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nostalgia for the future
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern intellectuals may replace nostalgia for the past with a 'nostalgia for the future'—an endless, receding horizon of expectation that is continually revised and never realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to rhetorical forms that valorize an imagined future in ways analogous to romanticizing the past. Such nostalgia can depoliticize present struggles by promising compensation in a perpetually deferred tomorrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial cooptation of countercultural or prophetic rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements (e.g., the counterculture) often operate as extensions of existing entertainment and leisure industries so that prophetic language is commodified while profits and cultural power are captured by industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims of cultural regeneration or grassroots revolution, examine structural economic relationships: who profits, who controls distribution, and whether symbolic promises translate into substantive institutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of ideological masking by technical rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical language and rhetoric (e.g., ‘information’, ‘feedback’, ‘systems’) can mask underlying political factors of class, status, and power and present social problems as technical rather than political.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate technical claims into political terms: ask what social interests are served, what values are embedded, and whether 'technical' solutions are being proposed to avoid political contestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms embedded in information systems (metainformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information systems contain metainformational content—programs, codes, statistical devices, retrieval schemes—that embody paradigms and value-laden rationales which shape what counts as information and how it will be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate software, databases, retrieval codes, and analytical devices for their implicit assumptions and biases. Consider how design choices privilege certain categories of knowledge and marginalize others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of communication from transportation as transformative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A crucial measure of a communications innovation's significance is whether it permits the separation of communication from transportation (the telegraph made message transmission independent of physical movement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the separation-test: technologies that decouple symbolic transmission from physical conveyance tend to reconfigure spatial/temporal relations and have broad social/institutional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of a signal as engineering criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern communications engineering centers on the 'economy of a signal'—the accurate reproduction and efficient transmission of a signal rather than merely energy economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess communications technologies on signal fidelity, reproduction accuracy, and information processing capabilities rather than only on energy or transport metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational and legal consequences (monopoly capitalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies like the telegraph create new organizational forms (monopolies, centralized corporations) and demand new law, management techniques, and legitimating ideologies for their institutionalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how a technology shapes or requires changes in corporate organization, legal frameworks, and managerial praxis; evaluate claims about decentralization against the institutional realities created by deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and cognitive effects of communication technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication innovations alter the nature of language, ordinary knowledge, and structures of awareness—e.g., telegraphy spawned new forms of reporting and conceptions of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a technology, trace its effects on discourse, genres, reporting practices, attention spans, and cognitive habits, not only on institutions and markets.
